checks.expected: We report on a father and daughter with stiff-man syndrome (SMS) and GAD65 antibody (Ab). The family had multiple thyrogastric autoimmune disorders; type-1 diabetes, thyroiditis, and pernicious anemia appearing as dominant traits. The propositus had pernicious anemia and thyroiditis. At age 53 years, neurological symptoms and signs developed, consistent with SMS limited to one limb. GAD65Ab was 199 nmol/L (normal, #0.02 nmol/L). Azathioprine and diazepam reduced limb spasms and GAD65Ab (12.9 nmol/L). Classic SMS began in the daughter at age 31 years, progressing to episodic opisthotonos. Baclofen relieved symptoms. She had GAD65Ab (88.7 nmol/L) and thyroperoxidase Ab (100 IU/ ml; normal, ,20 IU/ml) but no clinical thyroiditis. Her asymptomatic daughter acquired GAD65Ab transplacentally (72.7 nmol/L at birth; 6.65 nmol/L at 3 months; 0.65 nmol/L at 7 months). SMS is usually sporadic, frequently coexisting with thyrogastric autoimmunity. Three families have been reported with congenital SMS. These cases antedated GAD65Ab testing and differed clinically from acquired SMS. Stiffness presented at birth, dysphagia was prominent, and facial muscles were involved. No coexisting autoimmune disorders were reported. Our report illustrates that SMS, like associated thyrogastric disorders, occurs in families as a dominant trait. Immunogenetic determinants of familial SMS may involve a common mutation responsible for abrogating self-tolerance in all of the associated but autoantigen-distinct disorders.
